metadata.title: PISA 2009 Results: What Students Know and Can Do (EN) – Volume I

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report is based on the PISA 2009 international assessment of 15-year-olds across 65 participating countries and economies, using a complex two-stage sampling design (schools, then students within schools) with strict participation/exclusion rules to preserve comparability. The report describes that school principal questionnaire responses are weighted to be proportional to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in each school, indicating the use of sampling/coverage weights for school-level reporting. For student-level performance reporting, the report emphasizes that results are derived from samples and that exclusion rates are controlled to limit distortion of national mean scores. However, the excerpt provided does not specify the exact student weight variable names or any replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so the precise weighting implementation for student estimates cannot be confirmed from the text shown.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This volume reports PISA results and assessment framework information rather than training or estimating a predictive model with a specified plausible-values (PV) procedure. The excerpt does not document a PV-combining or PV-imputation strategy for any student-level achievement modeling step, so PV handling is not applicable to the extraction target here. Missing data are discussed only at the level of publication symbols (e.g., data not available/withdrawn), not as an analytic missing-data procedure (e.g., listwise deletion or multiple imputation), hence missing-data handling is not reported for analysis.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: PISA 2009 targets students aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months who have completed at least 6 years of formal schooling, regardless of institution type (public/private, academic/vocational, full-time/part-time). The report describes stringent technical standards for defining national target populations and permissible exclusions, with an overall exclusion rate within a country required to be below 5% to limit distortion of national mean scores. Exclusions are allowed for inaccessibility/feasibility reasons at the school level and for intellectual disability, functional disability, or limited proficiency in the language of the assessment at the student level, with additional caps (e.g., school-level exclusions for disability/language not exceeding 2% and within-school exclusions not exceeding 2.5%). The excerpt does not provide the exact analytic-sample filtering steps used for any specific table/figure beyond these population and exclusion rules.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD volume reports descriptive and comparative results from PISA 2009, focusing on reading literacy (with updates for mathematics and science). The assessment was administered to around 470,000 students in 2009 across 65 participating countries and economies, with a second round in 2010 for additional partners. Each student completed a two-hour pencil-and-paper assessment with randomly assigned test booklets (13 booklets per country), covering reading, mathematics, and science, and a questionnaire (~30 minutes) for student background, learning habits, attitudes, engagement, and motivation; school principals also completed a school questionnaire. Reading literacy is reported on a proficiency scale (OECD mean set at 500 in PISA 2000, SD 100) with seven levels, and results are further broken down by aspects (access/retrieve; integrate/interpret; reflect/evaluate) and text formats (continuous; non-continuous). The report emphasizes that PISA cannot identify cause-and-effect relationships, but it provides policy-relevant benchmarks and trend information under controlled sampling and exclusion standards.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is for an OECD PISA results volume rather than an empirical ML study. The excerpt provides assessment design, sampling/exclusion rules, and descriptive benchmarks (e.g., proficiency levels, gender gaps, country mean scores), but it does not specify any predictive modeling pipeline, target variables, or ML algorithms. Consequently, main_findings and confounders_identified are empty by design, and PV/missing-data handling are not documented as analytic procedures for a model.
